reason: The transporter-bearing cell and arriving glucose suggest the next step is to bring fuel into the cell.
expectation: Glucose and oxygen will become available inside the cell for energy production.

effect: The cell combines with the muscle fibre structures to form the scaffold, so fuel was not the immediate pairing.
reaction: I was surprised that the cell first became the fibre scaffold.
reason: The thin and thick filaments appear to be the complementary parts of the fibre's contractile units.
expectation: They will form a contractile unit that can be added to the muscle fibre.

effect: The thin and thick filaments formed sliding filament units, which appear ready to fit into the muscle fibre.
reaction: The overlapping filaments make their relationship clear.
reason: The fibre scaffold has spaces for contractile units, so the sliding filament units should fit there.
expectation: The sliding filament units will be installed in the muscle fibre.

effect: The sliding filament units are now installed in the muscle fibre. The remaining goal is to make it pull and relax.
reaction: The scaffold and filament assembly fit together clearly.
reason: Glucose and oxygen are fuel inputs, and mitochondria are associated with making usable energy.
expectation: This will start energy production needed for the fibre to work.

effect: Glucose and oxygen fuelled the mitochondria; ADP and phosphate appear to be the remaining inputs for making ATP.
reaction: The picture clarified that glucose is first split in the cell fluid.
reason: ADP and phosphate are the materials needed to make ATP, the usable energy mentioned in the chapter intro.
expectation: The fuelled mitochondria will produce ATP from ADP and phosphate.

effect: The fuelled mitochondria produced an ATP supply, which can support the fibre's pulling machinery.
reaction: The returning ADP and phosphate make the repeated supply of ATP clearer.
reason: The filament-filled fibre needs ATP for its pulling machinery, so these pieces appear ready to combine.
expectation: The ATP supply will equip the fibre's filaments to pull.

effect: The fibre is now ATP-ready, but the binding site remains covered, suggesting it still needs a signal before pulling.
reaction: The two frames make ATP's role in releasing and resetting the myosin head clearer.
reason: The calcium signal appears to be the next input needed to let the filaments interact.
expectation: Calcium will uncover the binding sites and allow the fibre to pull.

effect: Calcium exposed the grip sites, allowing the filaments to slide and the fibre to shorten. The fibre still needs to relax.
reaction: The distinction between the fibre shortening and the filaments sliding is clear.
reason: The calcium-pumping membranes appear able to remove calcium from around the filaments so the fibre can relax.
expectation: Calcium will be pumped back into storage, allowing the fibre to relax and become ready for another pull.

effect: Pumping calcium back into storage covered the grip sites and stopped pulling, completing the pull-and-relax cycle. The result also showed that relaxation requires ATP.
reaction: I found it interesting that relaxation also needs cellular work.

mostWorthwhile.text: Making the fibre shorten was most worthwhile: the paired poses and explanation connected calcium's signal to sliding filaments and clarified that the filaments themselves do not shorten.

leastWorthwhile.text: The initial attempt to bring fuel into the cell was the most confusing passage. The automatic combination produced the fibre scaffold, but the reason fuel could not be combined with the cell at that point was not clear from the board.

surprise.text: I was surprised that relaxation requires ATP-powered pumps to return calcium to storage, rather than simply stopping the signal.

arbitrary.text: The required pairing of the transporter-bearing cell with muscle fibre structures felt somewhat arbitrary at first; the descriptions suggested a relationship, but not that it had to come before combining the cell with fuel.

continue.text: I would choose to continue because the chapter linked fuel, ATP, calcium and filament movement into a useful sequence, and I am curious how the fibre will connect to a larger body system.
